name: Anishininew
packetScope: Three substantive inspected works: renewed KI community history, Sandy Lake's community welcome/history guide, and KI's 2018 public Senate testimony. One partially inspected scholarly introduction is retained outside the substantive count after deeper access failed. No canonical/Site edits, contact or delegation.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Big Trout Lake's local historical account
claimBlocks.text: KI's history places Anishinewuk families around Big Trout Lake within relationships sustained through seasonal gatherings and shared responsibilities. It dates the local Treaty 9 adhesion to July 5, 1929 and records elders' understanding that people would retain authority over customary lands and resources. The account then follows settlements developing separate administrations. These are KI's historical narrative and oral understandings, rather than a single history or present legal rule for every Anishininew community.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Sandy Lake's connections and public memory
claimBlocks.text: Sandy Lake's 2017–18 welcome guide recalls connections with Deer Lake, North Spirit Lake and Keewaywin. Its historical account links family movement and settlement with changing band administration. The timeline also remembers the 2010 Treaty 5 centenary through community events and a painting by Bart Meekis and Robert Kakegamic. This is a particular community's dated account, showing why neighboring nations' histories and political institutions should remain distinct.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Printed 2–5 (PDF 3–6), particularly welcome letter 2 and timeline 5

claimBlocks.text: In 2018 Senate testimony, KI's Donald Morris described documenting elders' knowledge of the 1929 treaty relationship. His account connected this historical work with community declarations and governance planning. He presented treaty-making as an ongoing relationship requiring renewal and reciprocal respect. This public statement shows a community actively recording and interpreting its history; it is testimony about KI's understanding, not a finding that its interpretation matches every Crown document or another nation's account.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A partially inspected scholarly reading lead
claimBlocks.text: Ariss and Cutfeet's 2011 introduction frames KI's mining dispute as a meeting of different legal systems and asks whether courts recognized the community's own law. Cutfeet's author note identifies his earlier KI lands-and-environment role. Only these opening pages were inspected before deeper access failed. The article remains a reading lead for its detailed analysis, rather than an additional fully reviewed historical work or present legal guidance.

The page's generic 1905 Moose Factory wording is not adopted. Its older 1996 declaration and current Island Lake preferred identity must not be conflated.

integrationNotes: Renew p15-s6 using an15-h1, preserving its original URL/provenance; this is one renewal, not another new count.

Replace the old KI paragraph with its scoped new block rather than appending duplicate source-derived prose. Remove p15-s6 from the Wasagamack-specific identity paragraph unless a precise KI-supported statement is separately identified; two full paragraphs could exceed the 180-word budget.

These works use local/historical names. Sandy Lake's 2017–18 Oji-Cree/Anishinabek vocabulary and KI's Anishinewuk/older-declaration names do not override present Island Lake preferences or establish identical peoplehood by language alone.

One community guide, one KI history page and one dated Senate proceeding each count once. Do not separately count the linked old website, declarations, affidavit project, painting, maps, or journal landing/PDF routes.

Claim blocks deliberately stay below 75 words and combined annotation+scope+block below 180. Recompute if an overview or other section also cites a source. The partial Ariss/Cutfeet card may remain only a research lead if root prefers three public main cards.
